survived.verified_statement: In notebooks/66_optimal_policy_cgg1999_replication.py, and identically in _es.py, every cell that calls record() ends with `assert all(c["max_error"] < c["tolerance"] for c in checks)` (lines 165, 209, 262, 327 and 382). No check is added between line 382 and the scorecard cell (lines 390-395). So in any top-to-bottom run (the jupytext build, Run All, CI), `scorecard["passed"].all()` is always True by the time line 393 runs. The `"NOT reproduced"` branch and the line-395 assert are dead code. A failing check stops the run at its own section with an AssertionError that carries no message. Only section 1 prints the checks table before its assert (line 163); sections 2-5 do not, so a failure there never shows which row failed. The only way to reach the branch is to run the scorecard cell by hand in interactive Jupyter after skipping a failed cell. The prose at line 387 ("The verdict line is computed from the table") and line 27 is literally true, but that computation can never give any other answer. Suggested fix: remove the five cumulative `assert all(...)` lines and keep the section-specific asserts (converged, gamma_pi > 1, FOC coefficients, price level, conditional ratio). survived.title: Named 'likely sources' of the Huggett and Aiyagari gaps are contradicted by the papers' own text
survived.claim: 'Where the originals and today's solutions part, the likely sources are in the papers' own descriptions of their methods: Aiyagari measured average assets from 10,000 simulated draws, and Huggett used 150 to 350 grid points with a clearing tolerance of 0.0025.'
survived.evidence: The same Huggett paragraph (JEDC 17, p. 962, read from the liuyanecon.com scan) says: 'With this criterion, interest rates that are approximately market clearing vary by less than a tenth of one percent.' I reused the notebook's own EGM and Young-lottery code (scratch t3_huggett.py) to compute the mean credit balance at each published q. It is +0.025 at (1.5,-2), +0.878 at (1.5,-4), +1.10 at (1.5,-6), +4.98 at (1.5,-8), +0.032 at (3,-2), +0.451 at (3,-4), +0.918 at (3,-6) and +4.70 at (3,-8). That is 10x to 1990x Huggett's 0.0025 criterion, so the tolerance cannot explain the gaps. Moving his grid top to a=4 (Kirkby's choice) shifts q by at most 1e-4. For Aiyagari, footnote 35 (p. 677) says 'We repeated all the calculations using 20,000 draws and found that the changes in the results were very minor'. The notebook leaves this out. My simulation of his single-series estimator (t5_mc.py, 200 replications) does make his gaps plausible: the implied rate has an s.d. of 0.173/0.150/0.113/0.096 pp at (0.4,0.9,5)/(0.4,0.9,3)/(0.2,0.9,5)/(0.4,0.3,5), against gaps of 0.256/0.222/0.146/0.128. The Aiyagari attribution is plausible but was never computed; the Huggett one is refuted.
survived.fix: Compute and print the excess demand at each published Huggett price next to the 0.0025 criterion, and call the Huggett gap unexplained (not the tolerance). Quote footnote 35 and p. 962. Add the Monte Carlo error of a 10,000-draw time average as a computed row, so the Aiyagari attribution becomes evidence rather than an assertion.
survived.verified_statement:

survived.title: The math cell puts Huggett's credit limit in the generic (1+r) budget
survived.claim: The shared problem c_t+a_{t+1}=(1+r)a_t+w z_t with a_{t+1} ≥ \underline a is presented as covering Huggett, with q=1/(1+r).
survived.evidence: Huggett's budget is c+qa'=a+e with a' ≥ ā on the bond's face value. In the (1+r) form the constraint becomes x' ≥ q·ā, which depends on the price. The code docstring says so correctly (:123-124) and the code sets `lo = q * limit`.

survived.verified_statement: The math cell (67_bewley_classics_replication.py:31-33, and the same text in _es.py:31-33 and both .ipynb) gives one budget, c_t + a_{t+1} = (1+r)a_t + w z_t with a_{t+1} >= underline a, and says it covers Huggett with q = 1/(1+r). That reading is wrong. Fix: in the math cell, write Huggett's budget as c + q a' = a + e, a' >= a_bar, and add that the code solves it as c + x' = (1+r)x + e with x = q a' and x' >= q a_bar. survived.title: Your-turn assertion is unfalsifiable: brentq's bracket already enforces it
survived.claim: 'The assertions check that the equilibrium rate stays between -δ and the rate of time preference' (:361); PLAN.md: 'the exercise assertion holds at the corners of its advertised ranges'.

(b) The distribution does not reach the top of the grid: marginal mass above 0.9·a_max < 1e-8. (c) Answer checks keyed to the prompts. Prompt 1 (width 2.5): round(cv,2) != 0.49 and r_custom > 1.5118. That is strictly inside the asserted (-8.0, 4.16667). If the root fell outside the bracket, brentq would raise ValueError before the assert ran. So the prose at :361 (es :361) says the assert "checks that the rate stays between -δ and the rate of time preference", but the real lower limit is -6%, enforced by an exception rather than by the assert. Three parts of the claim are overstated:
1. Every advertised knob setting gives rates of 1.5 to 4.0%, far from both limits. That covers Tauchen n in {3,7,25} with widths 1.5 to 3.5, and Rouwenhorst n in {3,7,25}. The (-8%, -6%) crash path cannot be reached from the exercise, so no learner sees wrong output or a crash.

The "Your turn" prompts (67_bewley_classics_replication.py:363-365; _es.py:363-365) only turn discretization knobs. Their answers pair a lower chain c.v. with a higher rate. Width 2.5 gives c.v. 0.4519 and r 1.8015%; n=25 gives c.v. 0.4167 and r 2.0833%; the default is 0.4885 and 1.5118%. The households become nearly permanent types, with high dispersion but almost no risk from one period to the next. survived.title: Explanations offered for the gaps are never tested, and the notebook's own numbers argue against simple noise
survived.claim: "the likely sources are in the papers' own descriptions of their methods: Aiyagari measured average assets from 10,000 simulated draws, and Huggett used 150 to 350 grid points with a clearing tolerance of 0.0025."

With excess-supply slope about 0.475 per 0.1 pp, that is about 0.02 pp of r, 13x smaller than the 0.256 gap. At the published r = -0.3456% the solver's excess supply is -1.20 (-9.6% of K). (3) Huggett: at the published prices the solver's mean balance is +0.45 (sigma=3, limit -4) to +4.94 (sigma=1.5, limit -8). If the 0.0025 tolerance is on excess demand, it cannot explain the price gaps; only a price tolerance could. I did not verify the 10,000 / 150-350 / 0.0025 figures in this session.
survived.fix: Print the excess demand at the published prices and the implied sampling error, say which quantity Huggett's 0.0025 tolerance applies to, and describe the gap pattern (systematic, growing with the precautionary wedge) before naming causes. Otherwise downgrade the sentence to 'unexplained'.
survived.verified_statement: Two parts of the claim hold. First, notebooks/67_bewley_classics_replication.py:352 (and _es.py:352) names method differences as the "likely sources" of the gaps but never tests them; line 382 admits it "relies on the published tables' own text for the method differences it names". Second, the Huggett half of that sentence is contradicted both by Huggett's own paper and by direct tests. Huggett (1993, p.962) puts the 0.0025 tolerance on excess demand for credit balances and says the resulting interest rates "vary by less than a tenth of one percent". The notebook's Huggett rate gaps are 0.25 to 1.76 pp. At the published prices the solver's mean balance is +0.025 to +4.98, at least 10 times the tolerance in every cell. (The reviewer's range, +0.45 to +4.94, leaves out the two limit -2 cells.) Huggett's grids (p.961: 150-350 evenly spaced points, spacing 0.03-0.1) do not explain the gaps either: at those spacings, discrete VFI moves q by at most 8e-5, against a gap of 0.003. The Aiyagari half of the reviewer's evidence is wrong. The reviewer treats the 10,000 draws as i.i.d., but Aiyagari (1994, p.677) simulates one household's Markov chain as a single 10,000-period series. At the corner cell the standard deviation of that time-series mean is 0.77, 8.3 times the i.i.d. figure of 0.096. That is about 0.165 pp of r, so the 0.256 pp gap is about 1.5 s.d., not "13x" the sampling error. Also, the notebook never calls the gaps "simple noise". Two parts hold and two do not.

What holds:
1. Line 354 overclaims in both twins (EN and ES :354, "which matches the income process exactly" / "que iguala exactamente el proceso de ingreso"). A 7-state Rouwenhorst chain matches only the mean, variance and autocorrelation of log income. Its distribution is binomial, not normal, and its level c.v. is 0.4097 against the lognormal 0.4165.
2. "Close to converged" (:354) and "seven states are enough" (:226) are never quantified. `seven_vs_25` is computed at :243 but never printed or recorded. But it is 15x the numerical error and larger than 15 of the 24 Table II gaps.

What does not hold:
1. Line 226 is not an overclaim. It already says "matches the mean, variance and autocorrelation of the AR(1) exactly", and the AR(1) is defined in logs.
2. The Q3 criticism (:365) is wrong. "Not depend on the number of states in the same way" is accurate. Rouwenhorst's level c.v. goes 0.397 / 0.4097 / 0.4148 for 3 / 7 / 25 states, while Tauchen's goes 0.601 / 0.4885 / 0.4167. The wording does not invite the answer "it does not depend on n".

- At :354, replace "which matches the income process exactly" with "which matches the mean, variance and autocorrelation of log income".
- Print `seven_vs_25` and record it in the scorecard.
- Reword "close to converged" to state the figures: going from 7 to 25 states moves the corner by 0.07 pp. That is small against the 0.81-pp chain effect, but as large as most Table II gaps, so the corner's decimals also depend on the number of states.

What holds:
(1) The Huggett case (puremacro/replication/cases_ha_dsge_causal.py:46-56, 118-130) uses a different endowment process from Huggett's. It solves huggett_steady_state with an annual 7-state Tauchen AR(1) (rho=0.9, innovation s.d. 0.2, so unconditional s.d. about 0.46). Huggett's p.960 economy is six periods a year with the two-state chain e in {0.1, 1.0}, pi(eh|eh)=0.925, pi(eh|el)=0.5.
(2) Aiyagari's sigma is the unconditional s.d. (his eq. 9). tauchen (puremacro/vfi/discretize.py:19-30) takes the innovation s.d., and aiyagari_steady_state passes sigma straight through (puremacro/vfi/examples.py:47). As a result, aiyagari_r_decreasing_in_rho (cases_ha_dsge_causal.py:41-43, 105-117) moves persistence and unconditional variance together (unconditional s.d. about 0.21 at rho=0.3 vs 0.46 at rho=0.9). survived.title: Transcription-identity checks hide their margins and verify only part of the digits
survived.claim: 'The printed tables check themselves ... within the rounding of the printed digits.'
survived.evidence: The Huggett row stores max(gap, 0.0), so the scorecard always prints 0.00e+00 and hides the actual margins: |diff| up to 0.058 against 0.08, and 0.122 against 0.53 for the printed '-23 %'. The slope bound uses 600*5e-5=0.030; the true 600*q^-7*5e-5 reaches 0.0314 at q=0.9935. The saving-rate bound 0.005 ignores the r-rounding term (up to 0.00025) and is met by 1e-4 at (0.4,0.0,3). Because ds/dr is about 2.3, the identity checks r only to about +-0.002 pp, so the 4th decimal of r is not verified. All 24 Table II cells and 8 Huggett rows do match the scans (OCR and page images of pp. 676, 678 and 962).
survived.fix: Print the signed margins and use the exact slope bound. Say the identity confirms r to about 0.002 pp, and record that the values were compared with the page images.
survived.verified_statement:
The margins behind the Huggett transcription check are hidden, and neither identity check can confirm Table II's r to its fourth decimal. In notebooks/67_bewley_classics_replication.py:145-146 (the same code sits at _es.py:143-146), the Huggett row records max(gap_huggett, 0.0) against a bound of 0.0. Both stored scorecards therefore print "0.00e+00 / 0.0" and hide the real slack. The smallest slack is 0.022 pp at (3.0,-4), where |diff| is 0.058 against 0.08. At (3.0,-2) |diff| is 0.122 against 0.53. The Aiyagari margin is not hidden: its row prints 4.90e-03 against 0.005, a slack of 1.03e-4 at (0.4,0.0,3). So "hide their margins" applies to the Huggett row only.

Both rounding bounds are approximations, but no check passes when it should fail:
- **Saving-rate bound (0.005):** it leaves out the r-rounding term ds/dr*5e-5, which is at most 0.000246. Leaving it out makes the check stricter.
- **Huggett slope term (600*5e-5 = 0.030):** the exact term is 600*q^-7*5e-5. That is 0.0314 at q=0.9935, so the check is stricter by up to 0.0014 where q<1. It is 0.0221 at q=1.0448, so the check is looser by 0.008 where q>1. Both errors are well inside the 0.022 minimum slack, and an exact interval check passes for all 8 rows.

Because ds/dr runs from 1.95 to 4.92, the saving-rate identity only pins r to about 0.001-0.0026 pp. It cannot confirm the fourth decimal of r, and often not the third, even though the rows are labelled "Transcription:".

Fix:
- Record the signed worst-case slack (or |diff|/allowance) for the Huggett row instead of clamping it at 0.
- Use the exact interval test: r_pub ± step/2 must overlap [annual_rate(q+5e-5), annual_rate(q-5e-5)].
- Either add the r-rounding term to the saving-rate bound or call 0.005 a conservative bound.
- State that the identity checks r only to about 0.002 pp, and that the full digits were compared with the page images.

survived.title: RBC mean shift is mislabelled 'precautionary capital'; the precautionary term for capital is negative
survived.claim: "risk shifts the ergodic mean above the deterministic steady state: households hold precautionary capital" (l.289); "the precautionary shift in capital is a fraction of a percent" (l.482)

The zero-shock fixed point (the risky steady state) is -0.0045% for k. Dynare 7.0's own ghs2 in tests/fixtures/dynare_live/rbc_order3.npz is -9.76e-05 for k and +9.76e-05 for c. So anticipated risk lowers capital, and the positive mean comes from the curvature of the policy (e.g. E[exp(a)]>1) interacting with realized dispersion.
survived.fix: Relabel it the 'ergodic-mean (risk-adjusted) shift' and print its three-way decomposition. State that the precautionary/risk term g_sigmasigma for k is negative here, as Dynare's ghs2 confirms. Retitle the panel, e.g. 'Mean capital under risk'.
survived.verified_statement: Notebook 68 attributes the RBC model's positive ergodic-mean shift in capital to precautionary saving, and that attribution is wrong. The shift is +0.0785% of k_ss at 1x volatility, and the notebook calls it "households hold precautionary capital" (l.289), titles the panel "Precautionary capital" (l.353) and speaks of "the precautionary shift in capital" (l.482). The same text appears at _es.py:289/353/482, where the panel title is still in English, and in both .ipynb files. The notebook itself defines the precautionary shift as g_σσ (l.18 "a constant precautionary shift at second order", l.34), and that term is negative for capital. In levels, g_σσ(k) is −9.76e-05 and g_σσ(c) is +9.76e-05, so anticipated risk lowers capital and raises consumption. Line 480 says "only an entry-by-entry comparison with an independent reference exposes it". That is false. The correct unfolded g_xxu has to be symmetric in its two state indices because mixed partials commute. So a reference-free permutation-symmetry check catches the planted error: the defect is 3.5e-17 on the solver's tensor and 2.6e-3 on the planted one. More generally, the errors a path check cannot see are exactly the non-symmetric part of a tensor, and a symmetry check catches every one of them. The error class behind the 20 September bug always falls there: REPORT.md:44-47 says "doubled one chain-rule placement" (2P instead of P+P^T), which gives an error of P-P^T, antisymmetric by construction. Line 39 argues that "a path that matches is weak evidence" on the grounds that "whole families of wrong tensors give the same contraction". Those families leave the decision rule unchanged as a function, so a matching path is strong evidence that the policy is right and weak evidence only about individual entries of the unfolded tensor. The notebook does say the error "cancels exactly" (line 232) and has zero effect on the path (lines 257 and 480). It never says the error also leaves every moment, stochastic steady state and response unchanged, and it never says why the error still matters. It still matters because the reported entries are wrong, for example d3c/dk da de in decision_rules(), and because it reveals a mistake in how the chain rule was assembled. Neither the notebook nor tests/test_dsge_order3.py checks decision-rule tensors for symmetry, so the title's "already catches it" means "would catch it". Fix, in both languages: (1) state that an antisymmetric error in a slot contracted with a symmetric product leaves every path, moment and impulse response unchanged, and that it matters only because the reported unfolded tensor is wrong (anyone who reads, folds or exports an entry gets a wrong derivative) and because it points to a chain-rule bug; (2) at line 480, replace "only ... independent reference" with "a symmetry self-check (mixed partials commute) or an entry-wise reference"; (3) at line 39, narrow the claim to "weak evidence that each entry of the unfolded tensor is right"; (4) add a scorecard row for the largest permutation-symmetry defect of ghxx, ghxxx, ghxxu and ghxuu, bounded at about 1e-14, and show that it flags the planted antisymmetric error.

survived.claim: "A path that matches is weak evidence that a tensor is right" (l.39); "Section 3 shows why the tensor comparison is the one that matters" (l.480)

The antisymmetric part the path misses is contracted with symmetric x(x)x(x)u products in simulation, IRFs and the pruned moments alike, so its propagated path change is exactly 0.0 and it changes no economic output. survived.fix: Say that matching paths pin down the symmetric part, i.e. the policy function, and that the invisible part leaves every simulation, IRF and moment unchanged. Name what it does break (reported derivatives, folded exports to Dynare/dynare++) as the reason for entry-wise checks.
survived.verified_statement:
The core fact holds, but the defect is an omission in the prose, not a false claim, and the reviewer's suggested fix overgeneralises.

What is true:
- The only path-invisible error the notebook demonstrates is the antisymmetric g_xxu error. It changes no economic output: the policy function, pruned paths, IRFs, GIRFs, the stochastic steady state and the exact moments are all unchanged. Every use of g_xxu in puremacro contracts it with x1⊗x1⊗u.
- The notebook never says this. Three lines let a reader think a solution whose paths match could still give wrong economics:
  - l.18 (and _es.py:18) says the risk terms "are easy to get wrong without any simulated path showing it". The risk terms are visible in paths: a 25% risk-term error moves the claim's path by 0.030.
  - l.39 calls a matching path "weak evidence".
  - l.480 calls the tensor comparison "the one that matters".

What the notebook gets right: its sentences are literally true about unfolded tensor entries, and Section 3 (l.234) states that the error "cancels exactly" in every observation.

Where the review is wrong:
- (a) The blanket fix "the invisible part leaves every simulation, IRF and moment unchanged" is false in general. The order-3 recursion contracts g_xx with the non-symmetric x1⊗x2 (pruning.py:1767, :1778). An antisymmetric g_xx error of 1.29e-3 is invisible in order-2 paths (1.1e-16) but moves order-3 paths by 1.67e-3 and covariances by 4.6e-4. Path invisibility therefore depends on which contraction is checked.
- (b) puremacro has no folded Dynare/dynare++ export. What actually breaks is dr.ghxxu entries read as derivatives, the decision-rule table exports (_results.py:733-748) and comparisons with Dynare's unfolded tensors.
- (c) The report citation should be reviews/2026-09-20-independent-validation/REPORT.md:46, not :44.
- (d) docs/notebooks.md:116 is accurate as written.

Best fix, applied at l.18, l.39 and l.480 and the matching lines of _es.py:
- State that the planted or real antisymmetric g_xxu error leaves the policy function and every path, IRF and moment unchanged.
- Say that entry-wise checks still matter for two reasons: reported derivatives were wrong, and the same kind of error in a tensor contracted with non-symmetric products (g_xx at order 3) does change outputs.
- Stop attributing path invisibility to the risk terms.

Across seeds 7-11 the z pairs are (1.41,1.40), (2.23,2.23), (-0.22,-0.21), (-1.31,-1.29), (0.32,0.34): one test reported twice.

survived.verified_statement:
The mechanics are right; two parts of the claim go too far.

What is true:
- The scaling row ("Risk-adjusted mean proportional to variance", notebooks/68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:305-306, :339, labelled "exact") holds by construction. Order3PrunedSolution.stochastic_steady_state (puremacro/dsge/pruning.py:1930-1966) scales Sigma_e by sigma^2 (_sigma_u, :1620-1627). Omega then scales by sigma^2 (the Lyapunov equation is linear) and H/G_sigmasigma are multiplied by sig2, so shift(m) = m^2 shift(1) exactly. The row can only catch an inconsistent power of sigma inside that one function. It is not an oracle like the other "exact" rows.
- The sigma=3 simulation (:309) is the sigma=1 draw scaled by 3. _draw_shocks (:1634-1637) uses the same seed with covariance times 9. Its second-order part is therefore exactly 9 times the sigma=1 one, so the "x3" z-score (:313, :316) and the x3 error bar in the figure (:350-352) add no independent evidence.
- The prose at :482 ("grows with the variance, exactly as the analytic formula says and within sampling error of the simulation") therefore rests on an identity plus one Monte Carlo draw. The Spanish twin (_es.py:305, :309, :482) and both .ipynb files have the same issue.

What is overstated:
- The statistical check can fail. It is a valid single test of the analytic ergodic mean against the pruned simulation at sigma=1. It just says nothing extra about how the mean scales with the variance.
- The scorecard records one statistical row (the max |z|, 1.4e+00), not two checks. The duplication is in the printed z line and the figure.
- The level of the shift at sigma=1 is checked independently against Dynare 8's pruned means for the 'rbc' case in section 5 (:408, :435). Proportionality to sigma^2 is a mathematical property of the pruned approximation. No number or conclusion is wrong, so this is an evidence overclaim, not major.

Fix:
- Relabel the scaling row as an implementation identity, or drop it from the scorecard.
- Draw the sigma=3 simulation with an independent seed (e.g. seed=1007), or report and plot only the sigma=1 z.
- Reword :482 (and its Spanish twin) to say the proportionality holds by construction of the pruned second-order mean, and that the simulation checks its level.

survived.title: In browser/no-fixture mode every scorecard bound prints as 0.0
survived.claim: Scorecard 'gives the measured value and the bound it had to meet'
survived.evidence: With the fixture paths removed, the run prints '3.3e-16     0.0       exact' for the 1e-12 bound, and 0.0 for the 1e-14, 1e-15, 1e-9 and 1e-10 bounds too. survived.verified_statement: The defect is real. When the Dynare fixtures are missing (the Pyodide playground, which copies only notebooks/NN_*.ipynb and not tests/fixtures), the no-fixture branches put the string "not run" into the bound column (notebooks/68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:227 and :444). That makes the column object dtype. to_string(index=False) at :467 then prints each float bound with pandas' default 6-decimal float format, so every bound below 5e-7 shows as "0.0". That covers 1e-12, 1e-14, 1e-15, 1e-9 and 1e-10; the z-score bound 4 prints as "4.0". Every exact row therefore reads as measured > bound (for example "3.3e-16  0.0"), which contradicts the markdown at :463 ("the bound it had to meet") and the printed "8 of 15 checks ran and pass". The assertion at :469 still uses the real floats, so the pass/fail logic is correct and only the display is wrong. The Spanish twin _es.py has the same code at :227, :444 and :467. The reviewer's suggested fix does not work as stated: in pandas 3.0.6 with index=False, a per-column formatter is skipped for float entries of an object column (checked). Fixes that do work: pass float_format="{:g}".format to to_string; pre-map the column, e.g. scorecard.assign(bound=scorecard["bound"].map(lambda b: b if isinstance(b, str) else f"{b:g}")); or keep bound numeric (NaN when not run) and let the verdict column say "not run". (2) The 'Risk-adjusted mean proportional to variance' row (:339, labelled "exact") is a tautology. stochastic_steady_state (puremacro/dsge/pruning.py:1930-1960) builds omega, sigma_e and sig2 all as multiples of sigma^2, so the ratio is exactly 1 whatever the tensors are. survived.title: Library: stochastic_steady_state returns the ergodic mean, which here has the opposite sign to the stochastic (risky) steady state
survived.claim: Method name and docstring: 'analytical pruned ergodic mean (second/third-order risk-adjusted steady state)'
survived.evidence: In the literature the stochastic or risky steady state is the zero-shock fixed point. For this RBC it is -0.0045% of k_ss, while the returned value is +0.0785%. The name invites exactly the misreading in the notebook's section 4.
survived.fix: Add an ergodic_mean() alias, document the difference, and optionally add risky_steady_state() (the fixed point of the pruned map with zero shocks).
survived.verified_statement: This is a naming and documentation defect. The numbers are right. PrunedDSGESolution.stochastic_steady_state (puremacro/dsge/pruning.py:730-733) and Order3PrunedSolution.stochastic_steady_state (:1930-1933) correctly return the unconditional (ergodic) mean of the pruned solution, as deviations from the deterministic steady state. The docstring body and the Series names ("ergodic_mean_states"/"ergodic_mean_controls", :790-791 and :1966-1967) already say so. The method name, and the docstring parenthetical "(second[/third]-order risk-adjusted steady state)", suggest a different object: the stochastic or risky steady state, which is the fixed point of the policy with risk switched on (sigma=1) and zero shocks. For the notebook-68 RBC the two have opposite signs for capital: the ergodic mean is +0.0785% of k_ss, the pruned zero-shock fixed point is -0.0045%. docs/dsge_build.md:300 adds to the confusion by calling the result a "Risk-Adjusted Ergodic Steady State" that "computes analytical precautionary shifts induced by volatility", and its example passes sigma=0.01, although sigma multiplies the shock scale. Notebook 68 reads the ergodic-mean shift as "precautionary capital" (.py:18, 289, 353, 482; the _es twin at :289 says the same). The zero-shock fixed point contradicts that reading. Recommended fix: add ergodic_mean() and make stochastic_steady_state a documented alias of it, kept for backward compatibility; theoretical_moments(pruning=False) at :865 relies on it. Add risky_steady_state(), whose pruned closed form is x = (I-G)^{-1} * 0.5*H_ss*sigma^2 and y = F x + 0.5*G_ss*sigma^2. At order 3 the zero-shock pruned x3 is 0, so the same formula holds; an unpruned variant would need a fixed-point solve. Also correct docs/dsge_build.md:300, and reword notebook 68 section 4 and its plot title so the +0.0785% is not called precautionary capital.

survived.title: The exercise assert re-runs a section-1 check that cannot fail in range; no prompt's answer is checked
survived.claim: "the assertion checks the solver's risk terms against the closed form" (l.489)
survived.evidence: Section 1 already runs this comparison at 12 calibrations. I ran all 8 corners of the ranges: every one holds, with largest relative error 1.9e-16 at B=78.407 (beta=0.99, rho=0.95, s=0.5). Values outside the range fail the range assert as intended (beta=0.999, rho=1.0, s=0.0, beta=0.4). Prompt 2 is well posed: from beta=0.95 to 0.99 at rho=0.95, B/s^2 goes from 149.7 to 313.6 (x2.09), driven by 1/(1-beta*rho) (x1.64) more than 1/(1-beta*rho^3) (x1.23). Neither prompt 2 nor prompt 3 is checked by any assert, and the stretch has no scaffold because claim_to_cube hard-codes the payoff.
survived.fix: Give each prompt its own assert. Add a claim_to_quad(beta, rho, s, c2) helper for the stretch and check ghs2 = 2*beta*c2*s^2/((1-beta)(1-beta*rho^2)) (tested; see exercise proposals).
survived.verified_statement:
The "Your turn" cell (68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:496-505, identical in _es.py) only compares the solver's ghxss/ghuss with the closed form at the reader's (beta, rho, s). Section 1 already checks this at 12 calibrations, every tensor, 1e-12 bound (lines 124-135, 166, 169). A correct solver passes it everywhere in the advertised range, so the assert is a regression check and cannot check any answer. None of the three prompts (lines 491-493) has an assert. The stretch has no scaffold because claim_to_cube hard-codes the x^3 payoff (lines 102-106).

The claim needs one qualification, and checking it turned up two more problems:
(a) The range is not failure-free. rho_claim = 0.0 is inside the advertised range (-0.95 to 0.95, lines 497 and 499), yet load_mod raises ModelError "no predetermined state variables detected" before the assert runs. |rho| <= 1e-12 does the same.
(b) Prompt 1 (line 491) rests on a false premise. With rho < 0, ghuss = 2B changes sign, but ghxss = 2B*rho = 6*beta*A*rho^2*s^2/(1-beta*rho) stays positive. An assert checking prompt 1 would have caught this.

The template (notebooks/_TEMPLATE.md:18-21) only asks for "an assert that holds for the default", so the reviewer's narrow point is a teaching weakness, not a rule violation. Point (a) does break _TEMPLATE.md:40, "Make exercise assertions valid for the advertised parameter choices".

Best fix:
- Rewrite prompt 1 to ask why ghuss flips sign while ghxss does not, and assert sign(ghuss) == sign(rho) and ghxss >= 0.
- Assert the prompt-2 decomposition: B/s^2 = 3*beta*rho*A/(1-beta*rho).
- Exclude rho = 0 from the range, or catch the case.
- Add a claim_to_quad(beta, rho, s, c2) helper and assert ghs2 = 2*beta*c2*s^2/((1-beta)*(1-beta*rho^2)), with ghxss and ghuss unchanged. I tested this at 3 calibrations; the largest relative error was 1.5e-16.

survived.title: The 'statistical' Dynare-simulation row uses an absolute 3e-3 bound, not the z-score the scorecard describes, and would pass Dynare's table on one model
survived.claim: "'Statistical' rows compare with a simulation and use a z-score bound" (l.463); the row bound is 3e-3 in absolute terms.
survived.evidence: Largest gap between Dynare's table and Dynare's own simulation: nonlinear_state 1.9e-3 (under 3e-3, so it would pass), quadratic_feedback 9.5e-3, correlated_cubic 0.145. Only two of the three simulated models discriminate between the tables. With Bartlett standard errors (T=4e6), puremacro stays within |z| <= 2.3 on every variable and lag. Dynare's table reaches z = 290 (correlated_cubic y, lag 1), 14.6 (quadratic_feedback y) and 3.7 (nonlinear_state y, lag 1).
survived.fix: Report per-model z-scores with a Bartlett or batch standard error, and a bound like |z| < 4. Also report the table-vs-simulation z so the scorecard shows which table the simulation rejects.
survived.verified_statement:
Part of the claim is true. The scorecard text says "Statistical" rows use a z-score bound, at 68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:463 and at the same line of the _es twin ("cota sobre el estadístico z"). But the row at :437, labelled "statistical", has an absolute bound of 3e-3, asserted at :439. The executed .ipynb shows that row with bound 3.0e-3. Only the other statistical row, at :340, really uses |z| < 4. So the description is wrong for that row in both languages.

Two parts of the claim are overstated.
(1) "Would pass Dynare's table": the row takes the largest gap over all three models. With Dynare's table in place of puremacro's values the row gives 0.145, well over 3e-3, so it would fail. The table passes only if each model is read on its own (nonlinear_state 1.92e-3). tests/test_dsge_order3_moments.py:222-225 already says so: "on nonlinear_state it is of its order".
(2) The z-scores and the proposed fix: Bartlett's formula assumes a linear process, and these pruned third-order processes are not linear. For nonlinear_state y it understates the standard error by about half. With a Monte Carlo standard error, Dynare's table is only |z| ≈ 2.0 from the simulation on nonlinear_state. A |z| < 4 bound would therefore still pass the table on that model. Only two of the three models can tell the tables apart, and that follows from the data, not from the choice of an absolute bound.

Best fix: change l.463 in both languages so it states each bound's type, e.g. "a z-score, or an absolute tolerance of about 3-5 sampling standard errors". Or turn l.437 into a z-score using simulation-based (batch or Monte Carlo) standard errors, not Bartlett ones. survived.title: Blind-spot cell contracts the tensor with total states, not the first-order states the pruned simulator uses

survived.title: Planted-error 'effect on a path' is a one-period contraction on total states, not a re-simulated pruned path

survived.verified_statement:
Section 3 of notebooks/68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py says it "measures what each does to a simulated path" (line 232). The figure bar is labelled "effect on a path" (line 274), the scorecard row is called "path effect" (line 252), and line 257 says "only the symmetric one reaches a path". What lines 244-250 actually compute is max|kron @ D.T|/2: the direct, one-period contribution of the planted g_xxu error, contracted with the total state sim.states. The pruned simulator (puremacro/dsge/pruning.py:1770,1781) contracts H_xxu and G_xxu with the first-order state x1_prev. The Spanish twin has the same code (lines 244-250 and 274) and the same prose at line 232 ("mide lo que cada uno le hace a una trayectoria simulada").

For example: pert = dataclasses.replace(rbc, H_xxu=rbc.H_xxu + D[state rows], G_xxu=rbc.G_xxu + D[control rows]), with the rows mapped from dr.variable_names to rbc.state_names and rbc.control_names, then pert.simulate(periods=2500, shocks=sim.shocks.to_numpy(), burn=0). The other option is to rename the quantity to "direct one-period contribution" in the prose, the table and scorecard rows, and the figure label, in both language versions.

survived.title: Section 4 proportionality evidence is weaker than presented: one check is true by construction, and the two z-scores share one seed
survived.claim: The scorecard lists "Risk-adjusted mean proportional to variance" as an exact check, and z-scores at x1 and x3 as simulation confirmation.
survived.evidence: stochastic_steady_state builds its result linearly from sigma^2*Sigma and sig2 (puremacro/dsge/pruning.py:1935-1955), so scaling_error=0.0e+00 holds by construction. Both simulations use seed=7, so the x3 draws are the x1 draws times 3. The second-order part scales exactly by 9, so the z-scores are nearly identical (+1.41, +1.40) and are not independent confirmations.

survived.verified_statement:
Both parts of the claim hold, in the English and Spanish sources.

(1) The "Risk-adjusted mean proportional to variance" row (68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:306 and :339) holds by construction, and the scorecard files it under "exact" next to the true oracles. Order3PrunedSolution.stochastic_steady_state (puremacro/dsge/pruning.py:1930-1964) sets Sigma_e = sigma^2*Sigma (_sigma_u, pruning.py:1621-1628). It then solves a Lyapunov equation that is linear in Sigma_e and adds 0.5*H_ss*sigma^2. So shift(m) = m^2*shift(1) for any code that plumbs sigma consistently. The measured error is exactly 0.0, and the reference is puremacro's own shift(1). That contradicts the replication card, which says "no reference value was computed by puremacro" (:23). The check still catches one kind of bug, sigma entering inconsistently, so it is not empty. It is an internal identity, not an oracle.

(2) Both control-variate simulations use seed=7 (:309). _draw_shocks (pruning.py:1634-1637) draws from N(0, sigma^2*Sigma) with the same RNG stream, so the x3 shocks are exactly 3 times the x1 shocks. The 2nd-order path therefore scales by 9 and the 3rd-order path by 27. Because the 3rd-order mean is negligible, the two z-scores (+1.41, +1.40) are one piece of evidence counted twice. The x3 error bar in the Precautionary-capital panel (:349-352) is the x1 point times about 9. So the "within sampling error of the simulation" sentence (:482) rests on one draw.

Fix: relabel the scaling row as a self-consistency or internal-identity check, not "exact" among the oracles, or drop it, and soften "exactly as the analytic formula says" at :482 (_es :482). Give the x3 simulation its own seed (e.g. seed=8). Alternatively, keep a single z-score and say that same-seed draws scale exactly (2nd order x9, 3rd order x27), so the second point is not an independent confirmation. Apply the same change to the _es twin.

survived.verified_statement:
notebooks/68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:305 (and _es.py:305) calls rbc.stochastic_steady_state(sigma=scale) with no comment. The prose at :289 and the scorecard labels at :339-340 call the object the "ergodic mean" and the "risk-adjusted mean". The method does return the pruned ergodic mean E[x2] and E[y]. It does not return the zero-shock risky steady state, and in this RBC model the two objects have opposite signs:
- Ergodic mean: capital +0.0785% above the deterministic steady state.
- Risky steady state: capital -0.0045%, i.e. below it.

A reader who reads the method name as the risky steady state would therefore misread the sign of the result.

Best fix: add a one-line comment at :305 in both twins, e.g. "stochastic_steady_state returns the pruned ergodic mean E[x], not the zero-shock risky steady state". Optionally print the risky steady state beside it: (I-G)^{-1}·0.5·g_ss·σ², or a long zero-shock pruned simulation.

Neither fits the numbers. The g_σσ term for k is negative, and the whole positive shift comes from the Jensen terms 0.5·H_xx·vec(Ω) and 0.5·H_uu·vec(Σ). The fix should reword that attribution too.

survived.title: Section 5 says the innovations are uncorrelated, then that Dynare drops a correlation, without explaining centring

survived.evidence: The key word is missing. The fixture note says Dynare's "uncentred innovation xf (x) u (x) u", and CHANGELOG.md:26 says puremacro uses "innovations centred on their conditional means". Without it the two sentences read as contradictory to a first-year student.

survived.verified_statement: Section 5 of notebook 68 (notebooks/68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:370 and :372, and the same text in the Spanish twin, _es.py:370 and :372) never says that puremacro centres its innovations. Both sentences use the same augmented state z_t, so a student has no way to see why the first claim holds and the second correlation exists. The missing fact is that puremacro replaces x^(1)_{t-1}⊗u_t⊗u_t with x^(1)_{t-1}⊗(u_t⊗u_t − vec Σ) and moves the conditional mean x^(1)_{t-1}⊗vec(Σ) into the transition matrix A. Its innovations then form a martingale difference sequence, uncorrelated with z_{t-1} and with all earlier shocks. Dynare keeps the uncentred term, which is correlated with past shocks through x^(1)_{t-1}. Fix: in both language versions, replace "uncorrelated over time" with a sentence saying this: each innovation is centred on its conditional mean (for example x^(1)_{t-1}⊗(u_t⊗u_t − vec Σ), with the mean moved into the transition), so the innovations are uncorrelated with the past. survived.title: AFR attribution: the centred, martingale-difference innovation is puremacro's reformulation, not AFR's
survived.claim: "Its innovations are uncorrelated over time, so theoretical_moments() computes the exact mean, covariance and autocorrelations (Andreasen, Fernández-Villaverde and Rubio-Ramírez 2018)."
survived.evidence: AFR NBER WP 18983 (fetched this session, p. 20): "z(3)_t is correlated with ξ(3)_{t+1}. This correlation arises from terms of the form xf_t ⊗ ε_{t+1} ⊗ ε_{t+1}". Its eq. (33) and the autocovariance formula carry explicit Cov(ξ_{t+1+j}, z_t) terms. puremacro centres xf⊗(u⊗u - vecΣ) (tests/test_dsge_order3_moments.py:127). The property the formula needs is 'uncorrelated with the current augmented state' (a martingale difference), not just serial uncorrelation. Dynare's uncentred innovations are themselves serially correlated, and that is exactly the term Dynare drops.
survived.fix: Write: 'Centring xf⊗u⊗u on its conditional mean makes the innovations a martingale difference sequence, so Γ_k = C A^k Var(z) C' + ...; AFR (2018) reach the same moments by keeping the uncentred term and adding Cov(ξ, z).'
survived.verified_statement:
Confirmed: notebooks/68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:370 and _es.py:370 (the same text is in both built .ipynb files) say the augmented state z_t is driven by innovations that are "uncorrelated over time" and cite Andreasen, Fernández-Villaverde and Rubio-Ramírez (2018) in the same sentence. That property belongs to puremacro's own centred system: the innovation xf_{t-1}⊗(u⊗u − vecΣ) is centred on its conditional mean (puremacro/dsge/_pruned_moments.py:14-16, :30-35; tests/test_dsge_order3_moments.py:137-138). AFR's third-order innovation ξ(3) keeps xf_t⊗ε⊗ε uncentred, and AFR state that it is correlated with z(3)_t. Neither the notebook nor the docs mention the centring anywhere, so a reader will think the uncorrelated innovations come from AFR.

One part of the reviewer's evidence is wrong. The claim that the moment formula needs innovations "uncorrelated with the current augmented state" and "not just serial uncorrelation" does not hold. In the stable linear system z_t = c + A z_{t-1} + B ε_t, z_{t-1} is a linear combination of past ε, so serially uncorrelated (white-noise) innovations already give Cov(ε_t, z_{t-1}) = 0 and the closed form Γ_k = C A^k Var(z) C' + C A^{k-1} B Σ_ε D'. The notebook's reasoning ("uncorrelated over time, so exact moments") is therefore valid for puremacro's system. Only the attribution is wrong.

docs/dsge_higher_order.md:103 (and docs/es line 103) is at most a nit. That sentence has no AFR citation and is true of puremacro's system. The AFR link comes only from the section heading at :79/:83, and the sentence just leaves out the centring.

Fix for notebook line 370 (EN and ES): "puremacro centres the innovation x^(1)_{t-1}⊗u_t⊗u_t on its conditional mean x^(1)_{t-1}⊗vec Σ_u and moves that term into the transition matrix. The innovations are then a martingale difference sequence, so they are uncorrelated over time, and theoretical_moments() gets the exact mean, covariance and autocorrelations from Γ_k = C A^k Var(z) C' + C A^{k-1} B Σ_ε D'. Andreasen, Fernández-Villaverde and Rubio-Ramírez (2018) keep the uncentred term, which is correlated with z_t, and reach the same moments by adding Cov(ξ_{t+1+j}, z_t) terms." In docs :103 (EN and ES), add "centred on their conditional mean" before "uncorrelated over time".

survived.title: Caveat section omits what the oracles cannot establish
survived.claim: The 'How comprehensive is this?' section lists only skewness and kurtosis, the 13-state limit and Epstein-Zin. The title promises perturbation 'you can trust'.
survived.evidence: Every oracle has at most 2 states and at most 2 shocks: the claim has 1 state, Brock-Mirman has (k,a), and the Dynare .mod files have at most 2 states and 2 shocks (npz state_names). So entries with three distinct state or shock indices, the permutation class of the 20 September bug, are never tested. In the Isserlis moment oracle x is linear, so x(2)=x(3)=0 and the xs, xrd and xf⊗xs blocks are untested; beyond Dynare's mean and covariance, they are checked only statistically. Approximation accuracy against the true nonlinear model is not addressed; tools/reference_validation/README.md says the benchmark does not 'prove approximation accuracy far from steady state'. All shocks are Gaussian, so g_σσσ is never exercised (it is also silently omitted from the formula at :33). A three-state closed form with correlated shocks, y=βEy'+x1x2x3, passes at 5.6e-17 in 9 ms (check3.py), so this gap is cheap to close.
survived.fix: State these limits in the caveat section. Say that 'trust' means implementation correctness, not approximation accuracy. Add the three-state closed form.
survived.verified_statement:
Most of the claim holds. The caveat section at notebooks/68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:510 (identical in _es.py and the built .ipynb) names only skewness and kurtosis, the ~13-state limit of the exact moments, and Epstein-Zin as future work. It does not say what the oracles leave open:
(a) Every oracle has at most 2 predetermined states and at most 2 shocks. So no decision-rule entry with three distinct state indices (g_xxx) or three distinct shock indices (g_uuu) is ever checked, and nothing checks the 6-way permutation handling that sits behind the 20 September mixed-derivative bug.
(b) The Isserlis moment oracle has a linear state. Its x^(2), x^(3) and xf⊗xs augmented-state blocks are therefore identically zero, and for nonlinear states those blocks are checked exactly only through Dynare 8's mean and covariance; autocorrelations are checked only statistically (3e-3).
(c) "Trust" here means the implementation matches the true derivatives, not that the approximation is accurate. Nothing in the notebook addresses accuracy far from steady state, although the repo's own README says so.
One sub-point is misframed: g_σσσ is not an untested term. puremacro specifies shocks only through a covariance and draws them as Gaussian, so g_σσσ is zero by construction, exactly as in Dynare's representation for symmetric shocks. Leaving it out of the formula at :33 deserves at most a clause ("g_σσσ = 0 for symmetric shocks").
Fix, in both language twins:
1. Add to the caveat that the oracles cover ≤2 states and ≤2 shocks.
2. Say the moment closed form has a linear state.
3. Say "trust" means implementation correctness, not approximation accuracy.
4. Optionally add the three-state closed form y=βE y'+x1x2x3 with correlated shocks. It passes at ~1e-16 in milliseconds.

survived.title: stochastic_steady_state() returns the ergodic mean, which the literature usually calls something else
survived.claim: The notebook calls this the 'analytic shift' and 'risk-adjusted mean'.

survived.verified_statement:
The library naming problem is real, and the numbers check out. The notebook part of the claim is overstated.

TRUE (library):
- Both methods named stochastic_steady_state compute the pruned ergodic mean: puremacro/dsge/pruning.py:730-782 (order 2) and :1930-1964 (order 3).
- Each is a Lyapunov-variance formula, and it returns Series named "ergodic_mean_states" and "ergodic_mean_controls".
- Both docstrings call the result a "risk-adjusted steady state" (:733 and :1933), and docs/dsge_build.md:300 calls it a "Risk-Adjusted Ergodic Steady State".
- In the literature, "stochastic steady state" and "risky steady state" mean the fixed point reached when realized shocks are zero, not the ergodic mean.
- For the notebook's RBC model the two have opposite signs for capital: ergodic mean +0.0785% of k_ss, risky steady state -0.0045%.

OVERSTATED (notebook):
- Section 4 already calls the quantity "the ergodic mean" at notebooks/68_third_order_perturbation_trust.py:289 (Spanish twin: "media ergódica", _es.py:289). So the suggested fix "say in section 4 that this method returns the ergodic mean" is mostly in place already.
- "Risk-adjusted mean" (lines 339-340) and "analytic shift" (line 316) are accurate descriptions of an ergodic mean, not misnomers.
- What the notebook lacks is one sentence saying that stochastic_steady_state() returns the ergodic mean and not the risky steady state.

The consequence the reviewer points to is real. The notebook reads the shift as "precautionary capital" (lines 18, 289, 482; same lines in _es.py). But the constant risk term that actually makes capital precautionary pulls capital down here. That is a separate finding.

Best fix:
1. In pruning.py:733 and :1933, and in docs/dsge_build.md:300, say "ergodic mean of the pruned solution", not "risk-adjusted steady state".
2. Optionally add ergodic_mean() and risky_steady_state() methods, the second returning (I-G)^{-1}·0.5·H_ss·σ² for the pruned states.
3. Add one clause at line 289 (and the _es twin) saying the method returns the ergodic mean, not the zero-shock risky steady state.

survived.title: Order-3 asymmetry row equals order 2 by construction
survived.claim: The table shows order-3 asymmetry 3.0e-02 and 9.5e-02, the same as order 2.
survived.evidence: All pruned third-order terms in a zero-future-shock response are odd in the impulse, so they cancel in r(+v)+r(-v): max |(up3+down3)-(up2+down2)| = 0.0 (check2.py).

survived.verified_statement: The numerator of the order-3 asymmetry statistic is identical to the order-2 numerator by construction. The responses start at the steady state with no later shocks, so the base path's first-order part is zero. Every pruned third-order term of r(+v)-r(0) is then odd in the impulse v: x1^3, x1⊗x2_base, x1⊗x2_v, sigma^2*x1, sigma^2*u, and so on. These terms cancel in r(+v)+r(-v). The printed ratio is not exactly equal, though, because the denominator max|r(+v)| includes the third-order part. At 3 s.d. the ratio is 2.95523e-2 against 2.95567e-2 at order 2 (relative -1.5e-4). At 10 s.d. it is 9.50872e-2 against 9.52381e-2 (relative -1.6e-3). The .1e format hides these differences, so the table shows identical rows (3.0e-02, 9.5e-02). Pruned through order 3, the symmetric sum also does not depend on sigma: the numerator is 2.7137949377e-03 at both sigma=1 and sigma=5. The notebook does not misstate the result. Line 482 (and line 482 of _es.py) already calls the asymmetry "a second-order effect", and neither the text nor the asserts at line 343 claim that order 3 changes it. The only problem is that the order-3 row suggests a third-order contribution that is structurally absent. Best fix: add one sentence after the table in both twins. It should say that pruned third-order terms are odd in the shock, so r(+v)+r(-v) is unchanged at order 3 and the order-3 row differs from order 2 only through the denominator. Alternatively, drop the order-3 row or print the numerator |r(+v)+r(-v)| instead. Optionally soften line 289's "third order makes them depend on the level of risk" so that it doesn't read as applying to the asymmetry.

survived.title: 'Relative' errors are absolute for small targets
survived.claim: Acceptance: 'Relative error below 1e-12 against the closed forms'.

survived.verified_statement: The main complaint is right, but the evidence overstates it. Every closed-form check in section 1 is labelled "relative": the card at :26 ("Relative error below 1e-12 against the closed forms"), the prints at :141 and :165, and the scorecard rows at :166-167. In fact every one of these checks divides the error by max(1, |target|) (:134-135 and :164). That makes it a mixed metric: absolute for any target below 1, relative above it. Most targets are small. For the claim to x^3, 51 of the 96 nonzero targets are below 1. For Brock-Mirman, 39 of 52 are, the smallest being 0.131. Many targets are exactly zero, and for those only an absolute error is defined. The claim that all risk terms are below 1 at these calibrations is false. At the calibration (beta, rho, s) = (0.646, 0.889, 0.461), g_xss = 2.797 and g_uss = 3.147, so those two are held to a true relative bound. No verdict changes: measured on nonzero targets only, the purely relative error is still far under 1e-12 (4.4e-16 for the claim, 3.4e-15 for Brock-Mirman). Suggested fix: in both language versions, relabel the card and rows as "error scaled by max(1, |target|) below 1e-12 (absolute for entries below 1, including zero entries)". Alternatively, report the purely relative error on nonzero targets and the absolute error on zero targets. Both would still pass.
